newsitem.title: PERU: Rats replace hostage crisis nightmare for residents.
newsitem.headline: Rats replace hostage crisis nightmare for residents.

text.p: With the end of the four-month hostage siege at the Japanese ambassador's residence, neighbours have discovered a new nightmare -- rats.

"I've heard that the place is full of rats, and since a week ago two were found in the cellar of my building," said Maricarmen Rosas, who lives less than two blocks from the bullet-ridden and burned-out diplomatic compound.
Peruvian commandos stormed the building on Tuesday, ending Latin America's longest hostage siege as they freed 71 of 72 hostages held by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) since Dec. 17.
But rubbish and rotting food from the 126-day drama inside the residence attracted the rodents, who first tormented the hostages and now bother the neighbours.
"In my neighbour's house one gigantic rat was found, so she's put traps everywhere. This isn't a joke. It's a serious problem, my husband is looking for a cat," Rosas said.

The affluent Lima district of San Isidro was a quiet place until the MRTA blasted its way into a cocktail party to take hostages, forcing area residents to squeeze past hordes of policemen, journalists and curious onlookers to reach home.
Rosas told Reuters that during the first month of the siege she could not get her car out of the garage and was dependent on taxis to move around town.

Even inside their houses, neighbours could hear the sounds of soldiers marching and music being blasted through loudspeakers as soldiers tried to wear down the rebels and disguise the building of the tunnels used to launch Tuesday's strike.
At night they lived with the stress that an explosion could go off and destroy all the windows of their houses.
But now, with the worst over, Rosas and her neighbours are buying poison to get rid of the rats.

Roman Catholic priest and former hostage Juan Julio Wicht said after being freed that "mice were all over us. This was so nauseous and disgusting that the number of rodents did not let us sleep ... we wouldn't sleep peacefully."
